title: Global & U.S. Prevalence
fact: Around 50 million people worldwide live with epilepsy, including roughly 3 million adults and children in the U.S.
explanation: Epilepsy is one of the most common serious neurological conditions on Earth — nearly 80% of those affected live in low- and middle-income countries.
whyItMatters: It's easy to think of epilepsy as rare. It isn't — you almost certainly already know someone living with it.

title: Lifetime Risk
fact: About 1 in 10 people will have at least one seizure in their lifetime, and 1 in 26 will be diagnosed with epilepsy.
explanation: A single seizure doesn't mean epilepsy — epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures.
whyItMatters: These odds mean seizures aren't a distant, abstract risk. They're a routine part of human health that most people will brush up against.

title: Stay. Safe. Side.
fact: The Epilepsy Foundation's core first-aid guidance fits in three words: Stay with the person and time it, keep the area Safe, and turn them onto their Side.
explanation: Most seizures last only a minute or two and stop on their own — first aid is about preventing injury, not stopping the seizure itself.
whyItMatters: You don't need medical training to help. Just these three steps make a real difference for someone having a seizure near you.

title: When to Call 911
fact: Call 911 if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or longer, a second one starts before the person recovers, breathing becomes difficult, it happens in water, or it's a first-time seizure.
explanation: Most seizures end on their own within 1–3 minutes and don't need emergency care — these specific red flags are what actually warrant a call.
whyItMatters: Knowing these exact triggers in advance means you won't hesitate — or panic unnecessarily — in the moment.

title: Not All Seizures Look the Same
fact: The International League Against Epilepsy classifies seizures into four main types — focal, generalized, unknown, and unclassified — spanning 21 distinct seizure types.
explanation: Focal seizures start in networks limited to one hemisphere of the brain; generalized seizures rapidly involve both sides.
whyItMatters: "A seizure" isn't one single thing. The type someone has shapes their treatment, their risk, and their day-to-day life very differently.

title: SUDEP
fact: Each year, more than 1 in 1,000 people with epilepsy die from Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) — the leading cause of death in people with uncontrolled seizures.
explanation: SUDEP is the sudden, unexpected death of an otherwise healthy person with epilepsy, with no other cause found on autopsy; risk rises sharply with uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures.
whyItMatters: Seizure control isn't just about quality of life — for many people, it's a matter of real, measurable survival odds.

title: Status Epilepticus
fact: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer — or repeated seizures without full recovery in between — is a medical emergency called status epilepticus.
explanation: The threshold for calling this an emergency has gotten shorter over the decades as research showed how quickly a prolonged seizure can become dangerous.
whyItMatters: This is exactly why "5 minutes" is the line seizure first-aid guidance draws for calling 911 — it's not an arbitrary number.

title: The Diagnosis Gap
fact: U.S. data show a median of about 19 months between a first seizure and a formal epilepsy diagnosis.
explanation: Delays happen at every step — deciding to seek care, getting referred to a specialist, and actually being seen — and a single normal EEG can't rule epilepsy out.
whyItMatters: Faster diagnosis means faster access to treatment that actually works. This delay is a real, fixable gap in how care is delivered.

title: The Treatment Gap
fact: Up to 70% of people with epilepsy could become seizure-free with proper diagnosis and treatment — yet three-quarters of people in low-income countries don't get the treatment they need.
explanation: The biggest barrier to seizure freedom for most people worldwide isn't medical complexity — it's access to diagnosis, medication, and trained clinicians.
whyItMatters: A huge amount of unnecessary suffering from epilepsy is preventable with resources that already exist — they just aren't reaching everyone yet.

title: Drug-Resistant Epilepsy & Surgery
fact: About 30–40% of people with epilepsy have drug-resistant epilepsy — but for carefully selected candidates, surgery can lead to seizure freedom in up to 80% of cases.
explanation: Surgery becomes an option when seizures start in one identifiable, safely treatable area of the brain, after medications alone haven't worked.
whyItMatters: "Drug-resistant" doesn't mean "no options left" — it means it's time to talk to a specialist about what else is possible.

title: Neurostimulation Devices
fact: For people who can't have surgery, devices like responsive neurostimulation (RNS) have shown real results — about 3 in 4 RNS patients see seizures drop by half or more.
explanation: RNS continuously monitors brain activity and delivers a brief pulse of stimulation the instant it detects a seizure starting — often before the person even notices.
whyItMatters: This is the same category of device-based therapy that's part of my own treatment story — proof that "no more options" is rarely actually true.

title: DBS for Epilepsy
fact: The FDA approved deep brain stimulation (DBS) for drug-resistant epilepsy in 2018, based on 7-year trial data showing a median 75% reduction in seizure frequency.
explanation: DBS delivers steady electrical pulses to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, a brain region involved in how seizures spread.
whyItMatters: This device is part of my own treatment history — and a direct result of decades of exactly the kind of research funding this campaign supports.

title: The Ketogenic Diet
fact: Over half of children on the ketogenic diet for drug-resistant epilepsy see their seizures drop by 50% or more, and 10–15% become seizure-free.
explanation: The diet is high-fat and very low-carbohydrate, prescribed and closely monitored by a physician and dietitian — not something to try without a medical team.
whyItMatters: It's a reminder that effective epilepsy treatment doesn't always mean a new drug or a new device.

title: Rescue Medication
fact: FDA-approved rescue medications like nasal diazepam let caregivers stop a seizure cluster at home — in one long-term study, a single dose resolved 87% of treated episodes.
explanation: These are used as needed for a cluster of seizures outside someone's normal pattern, not as a replacement for daily seizure medication.
whyItMatters: A tool that works outside a hospital can mean the difference between a manageable bad day and an unnecessary ER trip.

title: Common Seizure Triggers
fact: Across patient surveys, the most consistently reported seizure triggers are sleep deprivation, emotional stress, and missed medication doses.
explanation: In one survey of 546 people with epilepsy, 52% named sleep deprivation specifically as a trigger for their seizures.
whyItMatters: These triggers are largely modifiable — sleep hygiene and medication adherence are genuinely protective, not just good advice in general.

title: Photosensitive Epilepsy
fact: Only about 3% of people with epilepsy have seizures triggered by flashing lights or certain visual patterns.
explanation: Photosensitive epilepsy is more common in children, adolescents, and certain syndromes like juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and becomes less common with age.
whyItMatters: It's a common myth that flashing lights are a universal epilepsy trigger — correcting that matters for how media and venues think about accessibility.

title: Genetics Aren't Always Inheritance
fact: Epilepsy can have a genetic cause without being inherited — many genetic epilepsies come from a brand-new DNA change, not one passed down from a parent.
explanation: Researchers have identified close to 1,000 genes linked to epilepsy; a DNA variant can arise spontaneously with no family history at all.
whyItMatters: This reframes a lot of unfair self-blame and stigma — epilepsy isn't something someone's family necessarily "did" or "passed on."

title: Do Kids Outgrow It?
fact: Nearly two-thirds of children with newly diagnosed epilepsy eventually reach long-term remission — though outcomes vary hugely by the specific syndrome.
explanation: Some self-limited childhood syndromes resolve in the vast majority of cases, while others carry a much lower chance of remission.
whyItMatters: "Will my child outgrow this?" has a real, evidence-based, often hopeful answer — it just depends on which epilepsy they have.

title: Epilepsy in Older Adults
fact: New epilepsy diagnoses rise sharply after age 55–60, with one large U.S. study finding the highest rate of new cases among people in their late 80s.
explanation: Strokes, brain tumors, and Alzheimer's disease all become more common with age — and all three can cause epilepsy.
whyItMatters: Epilepsy is too often thought of as a young person's condition. It has a second, less-discussed peak much later in life.

title: Pregnancy & Epilepsy
fact: Women with epilepsy can have healthy pregnancies — medication choice matters, with newer options like lamotrigine and levetiracetam carrying substantially lower risk than older drugs like valproate.
explanation: Clinical guidelines now recommend avoiding valproic acid during pregnancy when clinically feasible, specifically to reduce the risk of major malformations.
whyItMatters: With the right medical guidance, epilepsy and a healthy pregnancy aren't in conflict.
sourceOrg: American Academy of Neurology / AES / SMFM

title: Mental Health & Epilepsy
fact: Depression and anxiety disorders are more than twice as common in people with epilepsy as in the general population.
explanation: A large meta-analysis found significantly higher odds of depression, anxiety, and several other psychiatric conditions in people with epilepsy.
whyItMatters: Mental health screening should be a routine, expected part of epilepsy care — not an afterthought to seizure control alone.

title: Employment & the ADA
fact: People with epilepsy are successfully employed as police officers, firefighters, welders, and construction workers — the ADA requires an individualized assessment, not a blanket assumption.
explanation: Under the ADA, an employer can only exclude someone for safety reasons with specific medical documentation of a real, current risk — not a general assumption about epilepsy.
whyItMatters: The barrier people with epilepsy face at work is too often stigma and assumption, not actual capability.

title: Driving Laws Vary by State
fact: Required seizure-free periods for driving vary widely by U.S. state — from as short as 3–6 months to a full year, and some states leave the decision to a physician's judgment instead of a fixed rule.
explanation: Most states require a doctor's statement about the date of the last seizure; some weigh the doctor's recommendation heavily, while others leave the final call to the DMV.
whyItMatters: These rules directly affect independence and daily life — and they're not uniform, so it genuinely pays to know your own state's law.

title: The Economic Cost
fact: Epilepsy and seizure-related health care cost the U.S. about $24.5 billion in a single year (2019).
explanation: That figure covers direct health care spending alone — it doesn't include lost wages, productivity, or caregiving costs.
whyItMatters: This is also a case for research funding: better treatment reduces this burden, not just the underlying suffering.

title: Caregivers Carry a Lot
fact: In a national survey, over half of epilepsy caregivers reported anxiety and 41% reported depression since becoming a caregiver.
explanation: The same study estimated the total U.S. economic burden of epilepsy caregiving at nearly $48 billion a year in direct and indirect costs.
whyItMatters: Epilepsy doesn't just affect the person diagnosed — it reshapes the lives of everyone caring for them, too.

title: Seizure Dogs
fact: Some dogs can alert to a seizure minutes before it happens, and trained seizure-response dogs have been shown in small studies to reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life.
explanation: Seizure-response dogs can be trained to bark for help, break a fall, or stay close during and after a seizure — but they're a support tool, not a substitute for medical monitoring.
whyItMatters: It's a vivid reminder that support for a chronic condition can come in forms you wouldn't expect.

title: Exercise Is (Usually) Encouraged
fact: The International League Against Epilepsy's own Sports Task Force concludes that physical exercise may favorably affect seizure control, on top of its broader health benefits.
explanation: Risk varies by sport and by how well-controlled someone's seizures are — the Task Force sorts activities into risk tiers rather than issuing a blanket restriction.
whyItMatters: With reasonable precautions, staying active — even training for something like a marathon — is encouraged, not forbidden.
sourceOrg: ILAE Task Force on Sports and Epilepsy

title: "The Sacred Disease"
fact: Ancient Greeks called epilepsy "the sacred disease," blaming the gods — until Hippocrates argued, around the 4th century BC, that it was a natural, brain-based condition, not a curse.
explanation: Hippocrates wrote that people claiming epilepsy was divine punishment were using that belief as cover for their own inability to actually treat it.
whyItMatters: Epilepsy stigma is nearly 2,500 years old — and dismantling it has been a project just as long in the making.

title: Why November?
fact: The Epilepsy Foundation has marked November as National Epilepsy Awareness Month since 1969 — Congress formally recognized it in 2003.
explanation: What started as one organization's annual campaign grew, over decades, into a nationally recognized month with its own congressional resolution.
whyItMatters: This campaign you're reading right now has more than 50 years of history behind it.

title: Why CURE Epilepsy
fact: Since 1998, CURE Epilepsy has raised more than $100 million and funded over 300 research grants across nearly 20 countries, aimed squarely at a cure, not just symptom management.
explanation: CURE Epilepsy was founded by Susan Axelrod and a small group of parents of children with epilepsy who refused to accept the treatment options available at the time.
whyItMatters: Every fact this month connects back to real, fundable research — and that research is fueled by people who choose to support it.
